description: Earshot NASA Space Apps Challenge group
summary:
We're Team Earshot, working on the health monitoring software for astronauts challenge. Our project is about proactive hearing monitoring and recommendations on space missions.

The problem: NASA rates in-flight hearing loss as a likely risk on the ISS. About 40% of in-flight hearing tests show a drop at low frequencies, and about a fifth of crew noise-dosimeter sessions went over the station's workday limit. NASA's minimum is one in-flight hearing test per mission.

Our solution: Earshot, a platform for checking your hearing during missions and keeping track of noise. You test each ear, and the app compares the result with your own baseline using NASA's definition of a hearing shift. If something changed, it asks you to retest, then shows where on the inner ear the change is and what to do next. There's also a map of the station with the measured noise level in each module, which alerts you to loud situations as they happen. A Today page checks your schedule against NASA's noise limits and acts ahead of time. For example, it reminds you to put in earplugs 15 minutes before a loud activity, suggests hearing rest after a loud day, flags a crew-quarters fan that's too loud for sleep, and moves your next hearing check earlier when something looks off.

It’s built on NASA data and on the Canadian Space Agency’s PRET data, which Earshot uses to tell whether a drop in an auditory memory test is unusual and whether a hearing change could be behind it.
details:
Earshot is a hearing and noise monitor for astronauts. You test each ear in the browser, and the app compares the result with your own baseline using NASA’s definition of a hearing shift. If something changed, it asks you to retest, then shows where on the inner ear the change is and what to do next, up to contacting the flight surgeon for a sudden drop. A station map shows NASA’s measured noise in each ISS module and alerts you to loud situations. A Today page checks your schedule against NASA’s noise limits and acts ahead of time: earplug reminders, hearing rest, an earlier hearing check.

The benefit is more frequent hearing checks between NASA’s formal tests (the minimum is one per mission), and fewer loud exposures in the first place. NASA’s high-frequency shift rule is the same one OSHA uses for workers on Earth, so the approach also fits noisy workplaces.

We built it with React and Vite, Three.js for the 3D station map, and the Web Audio API for the tones and the microphone noise check. We used Python to turn NASA’s raw data files into the app’s data, and Vitest to check the NASA formulas. It’s hosted on GitHub Pages and runs on a laptop with ordinary headphones.

Things we designed around:

  • Headphones aren’t calibrated, so the app only measures change from your own baseline and retests before flagging anything.
  • Cabin noise, so a microphone check runs before every test.
  • Privacy, so there’s no server and data stays on the device.
  • Earshot isn’t a medical device, so it supports the crew medical officer and flight surgeon rather than replacing them.
